message:
Gardening questions from a total beginner who took on a half-plot in September, sorry for the volume!

What's the difference between annuals and perennials, in a sentence or two? And can you suggest a name for my little allotment plot? My kids want it to have a proper name on a painted sign by the gate. I'd also love three easy vegetables to grow with kids that'll be ready before the summer holidays end.

The liquid tomato feed I bought says to mix 15 ml per 5 litres of water. My pump sprayer is a 2-gallon one, and it's an American brand so I assume that means US gallons. How many millilitres of feed should I put in a full sprayer?

What colour should I paint the shed so it blends into the hedge rather than standing out? The allotment committee prefers natural tones. And could you rewrite this note for the allotment noticeboard so it's less grumpy: "Whoever keeps taking the communal wheelbarrow and not bringing it back, please stop." I've been told I come across as a bit fierce.

Cheers!
response:
No need to apologise. Here you go.

## Annuals vs perennials

**Annuals** grow, flower, set seed and die in a single year, so you sow or plant them again each year. **Perennials** come back year after year from the same roots. Most vegetables are grown as annuals, while things like rhubarb and asparagus are perennials.

## A name for the plot

Some ideas for the sign:
- **The Muddy Patch**
- **Little Acre**
- **The Bean Scene**
- **Sprout Hollow**
- **The Secret Garden**

Or use your family name, as in "**The [Surname] Patch**." Kids often like seeing their own name on it.

## Three easy vegetables for kids

These are all quick, forgiving and fun to harvest. Sow them in spring:
1. **Radishes.** Ready in about four weeks, so kids see results almost immediately. Sow small batches every couple of weeks.
2. **Early potatoes.** Plant in March or April and dig them up from June or July. Digging for potatoes feels like treasure hunting.
3. **Sugar snap peas.** Sow in spring and pick in June and July. They're sweet enough to eat straight off the plant.

Courgettes are a good bonus: one or two plants will be producing by July.

## Tomato feed: about 23 ml

| Step | Calculation |
|---|---|
| 2 US gallons in litres | 2 × 3.785 = **7.57 litres** |
| Feed rate | 15 ml ÷ 5 litres = **3 ml per litre** |
| Feed for a full sprayer | 7.57 × 3 = **≈ 23 ml** |

If it turns out to be 2 UK gallons (9.1 litres), you'd need about 27 ml. Many sprayers have litre markings on the side, which settles the question.

Two cautions:
- **Check how the label says to apply it.** Most liquid tomato feeds are meant to be watered onto the soil around the roots with a watering can, not sprayed on the leaves. Only use the sprayer if the label says foliar feeding is fine.
- **Don't use the sprayer for feed if it's ever held weedkiller.** Traces can damage your plants. It's worth keeping a separate sprayer or can just for feed.

## Shed colour

A **muted sage or olive green**, or a **dark brown**, will blend best with a hedge. Darker, softer shades tend to recede, while lighter or brighter colours draw the eye. Most garden paint ranges have several "natural" greens and browns. Check with the committee first in case they have a preferred list.

## Noticeboard note

> **Communal wheelbarrow**
>
> Hello everyone! A quick reminder to return the communal wheelbarrow to its spot after use, so it's there for the next person. It's been going missing quite a bit lately. Thanks so much!

It's friendly and doesn't point at anyone. It also gives a reason, so others are there to use it, which tends to work better than a telling-off.

Enjoy the plot. September is a good time to start, since you have all autumn and winter to clear and prepare the ground before spring sowing.
